transcript.content: Good day, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in today?

Well, they brought me in because of what happened at the county fair. I was giving a talk about crop rotation, which is important, you know? Soil gets tired if you don't treat it right. My grandfather always used to say the dirt is like a bank account, you can't just keep taking out without putting back in. He grew the best sweet corn in the county. Anyway, during my talk, I climbed right up onto the big John Deere tractor they had on display. I kept jerking the controls, just yanking them back and forth, to show the crowd the 'new pattern.' It was a real specific pattern, you see. I just couldn't make myself stop, even with folks yelling at me to get down. They were so loud, but the pattern was just... it was right there in my hands. Did you know those new tractors have GPS in them now? Drives itself practically. Not like the old days when you really had to feel the machine.
Have there been times when you felt unusually energetic, excited, or irritable, where you were doing things more quickly or intensely than usual?

Well, sure, I suppose. Some mornings I wake up and it just feels like the whole valley is opening right up for me, you know? I'm out there just grinning at absolutely nothing, ready to tackle the whole day before the sun's even properly up. The sunrise over the east ridge is really something. Especially in late October when the leaves turn. We got mostly oaks and a few maples, but the maples are the ones that really give you that bright red. My grandmother used to tap them for syrup, but it takes about forty gallons of sap just to make one gallon of syrup. A lot of folks don't realize how much boiling that takes. You gotta stand over the fire all day, just stirring and watching the temperature. 

But anyway, yeah, I get all that energy going, and I'm moving fast, but then... if one of the hired hands questions how I'm doing things, or if my wife tells me I need to slow down? Heck, I just snap right at 'em. I get so riled up, it's like they just insulted the family name or something. And my family's been on that land a long time, so you don't do that. Four generations. My great-granddad bought it back in nineteen-ought-six. Paid next to nothing for it compared to what land goes for now. You try buying an acre today and the bank wants your left arm.
Have there been periods when you were much more active than usual, either in your work, projects, or other activities, where you felt like you couldn’t slow down or needed to keep going?

Oh, definitely. When I get going, I really get going. I'll be out there before the sun's even thinking about coming up, fixing the south fence line. Then, boom, I'm back in the shed recalibrating the sprayer, and then I'm on the phone with the suppliers before breakfast is even on the table. By noon, I've started five more jobs than any crew could ever hope to finish in a week. It’s just go, go, go. 

Speaking of the suppliers, you wouldn't believe the price of fertilizer these days. It’s highway robbery, is what it is. I remember when you could get a ton of urea for a fraction of what they're charging now. And don't even get me started on the delivery times. The guy who drives the truck, Hank, he’s a good old boy, but he’s always late. He's got this old hound dog that rides shotgun with him. A blue tick coonhound. Beautiful dog, really. Has a howl that could wake the dead. Hank says he uses him for hunting raccoons, but I’ve never seen that dog do anything but sleep on the dashboard. You know, raccoons are a real menace to the sweet corn. They’ll wait until the night before you’re ready to pick, and then they’ll just decimate a whole field. They have little hands, almost like human hands, so they just peel the husks right back... but yeah, I just can't seem to hit the brakes when I get in one of those moods. I just keep moving.

Have you ever had a period lasting several days or more where your mood was consistently much higher, more irritable, or you had so much energy that it was noticeably different from your usual self, even outside of your regular busy days on the farm?

Well, yeah, if you really look at it, those stretched-out times... the ones where I'm just charged up, not sleeping, going nonstop... they've taken up about ten months out of this past year or so. Ten months! That's almost a whole calendar year. Speaking of calendars, did you know the Farmer's Almanac has been published continuously since 1792? It's true. My granddad swore by it for planting dates. He'd sit there at the kitchen table with his reading glasses perched right on the end of his nose, tracing the moon phases with his finger. Said if you plant root crops in the waning moon, they grow deeper. Carrots, turnips, potatoes... potatoes are a funny thing. You cut 'em up, let the eyes dry out a bit so they don't rot in the ground, and then you bury 'em. I tried growing those purple Peruvian potatoes one year. Fancy things. The chefs up in the city go crazy for them, pay top dollar. But the soil in the lower forty is a bit too clay-heavy for them, they like it looser, more sandy. You gotta amend the soil with a lot of organic matter if you want a good potato harvest. But anyway, yeah, about ten months of the past year I've just been running on that high voltage, day in and day out.
During those times when you felt so energetic and couldn’t slow down, did you find that you needed much less sleep — like only a few hours a night — and still felt rested or even energized?

Well, sure, that's exactly how it is. Most nights during those stretches, I might catch two, maybe three hours of sleep, tops. Usually just sitting right there in my old recliner. Or sometimes I don't sleep at all. But I'm up before the sun, feeling completely charged up and ready to work the whole place like I just slept ten hours. 

That recliner, though, it's seen better days. It's one of those big, overstuffed corduroy ones, the color of dried mustard. My wife hates it. She’s been trying to get me to throw it out for five years now, says it smells like tractor grease and wet dog. But you just can't find a chair that fits your back like that anymore. They don't make furniture like they used to. Everything now is particle board and cheap foam that flattens out after a month. My dad had a chair he sat in for thirty years. Leather. Real thick leather. When he passed, my brother took it, put it in his basement, and it flooded the very next spring. Ruined the whole thing. It’s a shame, really, all that history just washed away because the sump pump failed. You gotta check your sump pump before the spring thaw, I always say. If you don't, you're just asking for trouble when the ground is frozen and the rain starts coming down hard... but yeah, just a couple hours in that chair and I'm raring to go.
During those times when you felt so energetic and couldn’t slow down, did you have thoughts racing through your mind so fast that it was hard to keep up with them?

Oh, yeah, absolutely. It's like... my head just runs so fast. Planting schedules, market prices, soil readings, and then all those messages I need to decode... it's like I can't catch one thought before the next one just shoves it right out of the way. 

Speaking of decoding, you know, the way the crows sit on the power lines out by the county road, it's not random. People think it's random, but they space themselves out based on the electromagnetic frequency of the wires. I started charting it. You can actually predict the weather patterns if you watch how close they sit to the transformers. Transformers are fascinating, really. Step-up, step-down. The whole grid is held together by these humming metal boxes. My buddy Earl used to work for the power company, climbing those poles. He got struck by lightning once. Swears it cured his arthritis. Said he tasted copper for a week straight, and the hair on his arms stood up every time he walked past a microwave. Microwaves, now that's a technology I don't fully trust. You put a frozen block of meat in there, and two minutes later it's boiling on the edges and frozen solid in the middle. Makes no sense. But yeah, the thoughts just pile up and race around so fast I can't even get a grip on them.
During these high-energy periods, did you feel your mood was unusually elevated or irritable in a way that was clearly different from your usual self?

Well, yeah, it's... it's like a switch flips. Some mornings I wake up and I feel like the whole valley is just opening up for me, you know? Like I'm standing on top of the world and I'm just grinning at absolutely nothing. But then, if one of the hired hands questions how I want a field plowed, or if my wife tells me I need to slow down and eat something, I just snap. I snap at them like they've insulted the family name. 

Family names mean a lot out here. My family's been farming this same plot of land since 1888. We've got the original deed framed in the hallway. It's written in that old cursive, you know, where the 'S' looks like an 'F'. You can barely read it unless you know what you're looking for. Penmanship used to be a real art form. Now kids just tap on screens. My grandson, he's twelve, he came out to visit last summer and didn't even know how to write his own name in cursive. I sat him down at the kitchen table with a legal pad and a good ballpoint pen—not those cheap plastic ones that leak, but a solid metal one my wife got me for our anniversary—and I made him practice. He complained the whole time, said his hand cramped. Can you imagine? Twelve years old and his hand cramps from holding a pen. But you know, he eventually got it. Wrote his name out real nice. But yeah, if someone gets in my way when I'm running hot like that, I just lose my temper completely.
Have there been times when you felt down, sad, or hopeless for several days or more, where you lost interest in things you usually enjoy, or felt like you didn’t have any energy at all?

Well, no, not really. I don't get down or sad like that. If anything, I'm just too busy. Always too busy. There's always a fence that needs mending or a tractor that needs a new belt. 

Belts are a funny thing, you know. You go to the auto parts store in town, the one run by old man Henderson, and he tries to sell you these new synthetic belts. Says they last twice as long. But I tell you, nothing beats the old rubber ones. They have a certain smell to them when they get hot, you know? Like burning tires, but sweeter somehow. It reminds me of the county fair back in '78. They had this demolition derby, and the mud was so thick they had to use a front-end loader to pull the cars out. My cousin Jimmy was driving a beat-up old station wagon with the doors welded shut. Painted it bright orange with a roller. He almost won, too, until his radiator blew. Steam everywhere. Smelled just like those rubber belts. Jimmy always was hard on machinery. He borrowed my chainsaw once and brought it back with the chain on backwards. I don't even know how you do that without noticing. You’d think the fact that it was just smoking against the wood instead of cutting it would be a clue, but not for Jimmy. So, no, I don't really get sad or lose my energy. There's just too much work to do.
Have you ever had a period lasting two weeks or more where you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, and lost interest or pleasure in most activities?

Well, like I was just saying, I don't really get depressed or anything for weeks at a time. I mean, two weeks is a long time. You can't just stop for two weeks out on the farm. If you stop for two weeks, the alfalfa goes to seed, the calves get out... 

Calves are escape artists, I swear. Last spring, we had this little black baldy, couldn't have been more than a week old. Somehow, he squeezed through a gap in the corral boards that I couldn't even fit my boot through. Found him three miles down the road, standing right in the middle of Mrs. Gable's prized petunia bed. She was out there with a broom, hollering at him, but he just stood there chewing on a mouthful of pink flowers, looking at her like she was the crazy one. Mrs. Gable makes a mean rhubarb pie, though. She brings one over every year for the harvest potluck. Her secret is adding a little dash of orange zest to the filling. Cuts the tartness right down. I tried to get my wife to make it that way, but she says rhubarb pie should taste like rhubarb, not a fruit basket. We argue about that every summer. But no, I don't get down in the dumps like that. Too much going on.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a major depressive episode (feeling down, sad, hopeless, loss of interest, low energy). My symptom profile does not include any symptoms of depression, as I have Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type) with manic features.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. I don't get down or sad like that. If anything, I'm just too busy. Always too busy. There's always a fence that needs mending or a tractor that needs a new belt. 

Belts are a funny thing, you know. You go to the auto parts store in town, the one run by old man Henderson, and he tries to sell you these new synthetic belts. Says they last twice as long. But I tell you, nothing beats the old rubber ones. They have a certain smell to them when they get hot, you know? Like burning tires, but sweeter somehow. It reminds me of the county fair back in '78. They had this demolition derby, and the mud was so thick they had to use a front-end loader to pull the cars out. My cousin Jimmy was driving a beat-up old station wagon with the doors welded shut. Painted it bright orange with a roller. He almost won, too, until his radiator blew. Steam everywhere. Smelled just like those rubber belts. Jimmy always was hard on machinery. He borrowed my chainsaw once and brought it back with the chain on backwards. I don't even know how you do that without noticing. You’d think the fact that it was just smoking against the wood instead of cutting it would be a clue, but not for Jimmy. So, no, I don't really get sad or lose my energy. There's just too much work to do.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a major depressive episode, which is necessary to distinguish between F31.8 (Bipolar II disorder) and F31.9 (Bipolar I disorder, current episode unspecified).
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period lasting two weeks or more where you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, and lost interest or pleasure in most activities?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a Major Depressive Episode (feeling down or depressed, loss of interest/pleasure), which is not present in my symptom profile as I have Schizoaffective Disorder, Bipolar Type without depressive episodes.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was just saying, I don't really get depressed or anything for weeks at a time. I mean, two weeks is a long time. You can't just stop for two weeks out on the farm. If you stop for two weeks, the alfalfa goes to seed, the calves get out... 

Calves are escape artists, I swear. Last spring, we had this little black baldy, couldn't have been more than a week old. Somehow, he squeezed through a gap in the corral boards that I couldn't even fit my boot through. Found him three miles down the road, standing right in the middle of Mrs. Gable's prized petunia bed. She was out there with a broom, hollering at him, but he just stood there chewing on a mouthful of pink flowers, looking at her like she was the crazy one. Mrs. Gable makes a mean rhubarb pie, though. She brings one over every year for the harvest potluck. Her secret is adding a little dash of orange zest to the filling. Cuts the tartness right down. I tried to get my wife to make it that way, but she says rhubarb pie should taste like rhubarb, not a fruit basket. We argue about that every summer. But no, I don't get down in the dumps like that. Too much going on.

inference.note: The patient has not endorsed any significant depressive episodes, ruling out bipolar I disorder, current episode depressed (F31.9). The clinical picture remains consistent with bipolar I disorder, current episode manic (F31.8).
